entry.title: Random forest model identifies Peruvian university dropout risk with 87 percent accuracy
entry.summary:
Four Peruvian university researchers built a predictive framework using the knowledge discovery in databases (KDD) methodology of selection, preprocessing, transformation, data mining and interpretation to flag Latin American university students at risk of dropping out. Their random forest model reached 87% accuracy, 86% precision, 85% recall, an F1-score of 85% and a ROC AUC of 0.91, outperforming the other approaches they tested, and the authors recommend it be adopted by universities for early identification of at-risk students.

Why it matters here: Provides PASS with a recent, fully open-access Latin American benchmark for a transparent tree-based classifier reaching strong accuracy on dropout risk, a useful comparison point for the models PASS will validate on Wits School of Education data, and evidence that KDD-style data pipelines translate well across university contexts.

Andrade-Arenas, Rubio Paucar, Giraldo Retuerto and Yactayo-Arias, IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI), 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Propensity score analysis shows a university scholarship cuts dropout odds by 40 percent
entry.summary:
Two San Diego State University statisticians compared five predictive models, lasso regression, a generalised additive model, random forest, XGBoost and a neural network, on 3,400 records of students at Portugal's Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre enrolled between 2008/09 and 2018/19. XGBoost reached the best F1-score of 0.904, with 88.2% accuracy and 94.7% precision, and random forest reached the best area under the curve at 0.935; a propensity score matching analysis then found that receiving a scholarship reduced the odds of dropping out by nearly 40%, equivalent to a 22.2 percentage point drop in dropout probability.

Why it matters here: Goes beyond prediction to intervention evidence, exactly PASS's next step of co-creating interventions with the University's Business Intelligence Services: it demonstrates a rigorous, quasi-experimental method, propensity score matching, for testing whether a specific support measure, a scholarship, actually reduces dropout once confounders are controlled for.

Romero and Liao, PLoS ONE, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Randomised trial finds human judgement still matters inside Georgia State's advising algorithm
entry.summary:
Researchers from Princeton University, Columbia Business School and Georgia State University's own advising team analysed a randomised controlled trial of Georgia State's algorithm-assisted advising programme. They found that roughly two out of three interventions advisers made in the treatment arm were expertly targeted using context the algorithm did not have, such as students' personal circumstances, financial factors and engagement, drawn from advisers' own notes, and that different advising styles were associated with different graduation rates.

Why it matters here: A direct empirical caution for PASS as it moves from prediction to co-created interventions with Business Intelligence Services and advisers: it shows that even a mature, long-running algorithmic advising system still depends on advisers' contextual judgement, supporting a human-in-the-loop design rather than a fully automated one.

Schechtman, Brandon, Stafford, Li and Liu, arXiv preprint, 2025 (accepted for ACM EAAMO 2025) · Working paper (arXiv preprint), co-authored with Georgia State University's own advising staff, accepted for the ACM Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms and Optimization (EAAMO) 2025 conference

entry.title: Predicting late postgraduate graduation at Makerere: 500 students, 71% finishing late, and a simple logistic model that matches the ensembles
entry.summary:
A retrospective modelling study used anonymised administrative records of 500 postgraduate students registered at Makerere University between 2017 and 2023, of whom 29% graduated on time and 71% late. Random forest, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and a stacking ensemble all reached similar accuracy of about 94% to 95% and ROC-AUC between 0.94 and 0.95, with logistic regression numerically highest at 0.950 and no statistically meaningful differences between classifiers. Being employed and older age at admission were associated with delayed graduation, while a higher undergraduate grade point average reduced the likelihood of late completion; the authors argue that interpretable models can match complex ensembles on structured educational data.

Why it matters here: A direct African precedent for PASS on the postgraduate side: the same outcome (timely completion), the same reliance on anonymised institutional records, and a finding that a transparent model performs as well as ensembles, which supports the project's aim of models that advisers and Business Intelligence Services can explain.

Lubelenga, Kivunike, Chongomweru and Ahishakiye, Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY)

entry.title: Inside the black box: student-success predictions are less accurate for racially minoritised students, and the usual bias fixes do not close the gap
entry.summary:
Using nationally representative data from the Education Longitudinal Study of 2002 and several machine learning approaches, the authors tested how accurately models built on commonly used features predict college success for different racialised groups. The models were less accurate for racially minoritised students, which the authors read as algorithmic bias inherited from historical data that captures societal injustice, including racism. They then applied leading bias-mitigation techniques and found them generally ineffective at removing the disparities in prediction outcomes and accuracy between groups. The American Educational Research Association named the paper the most outstanding article published in its journals in 2025.

Why it matters here: A caution PASS must design against from the start: accuracy has to be reported by group, not just overall, and the Wits models, trained on a South African student body with its own historical inequities, cannot assume that off-the-shelf fairness adjustments will fix disparities that the data carry.

Gándara, Anahideh, Ison and Picchiarini, AERA Open, volume 10, 2024; winner of AERA's 2025 Palmer O. Johnson Memorial Award · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC); AERA award for the most outstanding article in an AERA journal

entry.title: 11,698 first-year students and 69 variables: a random-forest early-warning model in Türkiye reaches 90.2% accuracy once the first-semester average is known
entry.summary:
Researchers from three Istanbul universities and a bank's business intelligence department built an early-warning system that classifies first-year undergraduates as likely to succeed or fail by the end of the year. The dataset covered 11,698 first-year students and 69 input variables; naive Bayes, decision tree and random forest models were compared, and random forest performed best with 90.2% accuracy. Models that included the autumn-semester grade point average performed dramatically better, and the student's programme and university placement examination score were the next most important variables. The authors propose acting on the predictions from the second week of the spring semester so that support reaches students before attrition occurs.

Why it matters here: A useful comparison for the Wits School of Education data: the finding that the first-semester average dominates suggests PASS should test how early a reliable flag can be raised, and the joint authorship with a business intelligence unit mirrors the project's planned work with Wits Business Intelligence Services.

Çırak, Akıllı and Ekinci, Higher Education Quarterly, volume 78, issue 4, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Wiley)

entry.title: From risk score to recommended action: prescriptive dropout analytics for 2,500 foundation-programme entrants in Ecuador
entry.summary:
Escuela Superior Politécnica del Litoral (ESPOL) in Guayaquil built a prescriptive analytics pipeline for a computing-oriented bachelor's programme, tracking 2,500 students who entered its foundation programme between 2020 and 2024, of whom 9.1% (228) dropped out. A Random Forest classifier using 58 features drawn from foundation-stage academic, socioeconomic and connectivity data reached a ROC-AUC of 0.95 to 0.97; k-means clustering split students into three profiles with observed dropout of 0.6% (high-resource), 5.7% (intermediate) and 25.7% (vulnerable), and the authors added SHAP explanations and counterfactual recourse tools (DiCE, CARLA, Alibi) to turn each score into a specific recommended action.

Why it matters here: Goes a step beyond prediction to prescription, the direction PASS itself wants to take once its own risk model is validated: a worked example of turning a risk score into an explainable, student-specific recommendation, and a profile-based reading of risk (by resource level, not just a single score) that the Emory-Wits team could test against its own Wits School of Education data.

Quijije-Castro, Peláez and colleagues, Frontiers in Education 11 (2026), open access · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Gradient boosting and 32 advisers: a deployed early-warning system evaluated for usability, not just accuracy
entry.summary:
Researchers at ISI Bali and Universitas Sains dan Teknologi Komputer, Semarang, built and deployed a web-based early-warning system on 1,240 student records from 2021 to 2024, combining institutional records with Moodle behavioural data such as weekly login frequency and assignment submission timing. A Gradient Boosting model, chosen after comparing four algorithms with stratified ten-fold cross-validation and SMOTE class balancing, reached 89.1% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.850 and an AUC-ROC of 0.931; 32 academic advisers then rated the deployed system on the System Usability Scale at a mean of 78.4, above-average usability.

Why it matters here: Most early-warning papers in this feed stop at model accuracy; this one also asks whether the advisers who receive the alerts find the system usable, a question PASS will face once its own model reaches Wits School of Education advisers, and the login-frequency and submission-timing predictors are simple LMS signals the project could test early.

Handayani and Priyadi, Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Information Technology (2026) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: 143,326 anonymised records, seven cohorts: an open dropout-prediction dataset from Tecnologico de Monterrey
entry.summary:
Tecnologico de Monterrey released a curated, non-identifiable dataset of 50 variables across 143,326 records covering 121,584 high school and undergraduate students from seven admission cohorts, August to December 2014 to 2020, spanning two educational models. The variables cover sociodemographic and academic information alongside institution-specific measures such as student life, and the dataset was built specifically so other researchers can train and compare dropout-prediction models.

Why it matters here: An open, ready-to-use dataset at a scale the PASS team is unlikely to match from Wits School of Education records alone; a natural benchmark for testing whether models built on South African data generalise, or a training set to trial methods on before running them on the School's own anonymised data.

Alvarado-Uribe, Mejía-Almada, Herrera, Molontay, Hilliger, Hegde, Montemayor Gallegos, Díaz and Ceballos, Data 7(9), 119 (2022), open access, CC BY · Peer-reviewed data descriptor, open access, CC BY

entry.title: OU Analyse: weekly machine-learning risk scores for every distance student, and a decade of published evaluation
entry.summary:
OU Analyse predicts each student's risk of failing the next assignment and updates the prediction weekly for tutors and student support teams, with the aim of improving retention across the Open University. The team has published on teachers' use and perceptions three years after implementation (LAK 2023), on co-creating an equality, diversity and inclusion dashboard to address awarding gaps (BJET 2024) and on a student-facing dashboard designed with students (LAK 2025, Journal of Learning Analytics 2025).

Why it matters here: A mature, evaluated system in a distance-learning setting close to much South African provision, with an open dataset the PASS models can be benchmarked against and a research track record on how teachers actually use predictions.

The Open University, OU Analyse (Knowledge Media Institute); Herodotou et al., Journal of Learning Analytics and LAK 2023 to 2025 · Institutional system with peer-reviewed evaluations

entry.title: Siyaphumelela: a national data-for-student-success network reaching 80% of South Africa's public university students
entry.summary:
Launched in 2014, Siyaphumelela works with post-school institutions to use data to improve access, retention, progression, graduation and work-readiness. It reports 20 partner universities, 80% of public university students reached, more than 1,500 university staff trained and R338 million invested, with an annual national conference and a focus on eliminating performance gaps by race, gender and socio-economic status.

Why it matters here: The South African ecosystem PASS sits inside: the institutions, staff and data practices already built through Siyaphumelela are the natural partners and audience for the Wits models and interventions, and the network's conference is a dissemination route.

Siyaphumelela, led by Saide in partnership with The Kresge Foundation (initiative site) · National initiative, funder-backed

entry.title: GPS Advising: more than 800 alerts, every undergraduate tracked daily, advisers who act the same week
entry.summary:
Georgia State runs predictive analytics over all undergraduates with a system of more than 800 alerts; when an alert fires, an adviser intervenes. The system went live in August 2012 and in one recent academic year generated more than 55,000 adviser-student meetings about specific alerts. Since 2012 first-year fall-to-spring retention has risen by five percentage points and graduating seniors take fewer excess courses.

Why it matters here: The best-known working model of what PASS proposes: prediction is only half the design; the other half is a person with time to act on each alert. Georgia State's alert-to-adviser loop is the pattern to test with Wits Business Intelligence Services and the School's advisers.

Georgia State University, Student Success Initiatives (institutional page) · Institutional programme page
